extracted.intended_audience: Coast Guard managers, contracting officers, program managers, and policymakers responsible for A-76 implementation and contract administration (also relevant to DOD/Omb/oversight auditors).
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for evaluating the effectiveness, administration, and cost outcomes of A-76 commercial activity reviews (management studies, PWS/MEO preparation, contracting, contract administration, and workforce impacts) in the U.S. Coast Guard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management study team composition (team effort)
rubrics_metrics.description: The management study should be a 'team effort' using persons with expertise in management analysis, staffing, position classification, work measurement, value engineering, industrial engineering, cost analysis, contracting, and technical aspects of the functional effort under study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GAO and the OMB supplement stress multidisciplinary teams; assigning the study as a collateral duty to an inexperienced individual is inadequate and lengthens completion time and reduces study quality. Lack of appropriate skill contributes to inaccurate PWS and MEO cost determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable timeframes for completing studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies should have realistic time requirements; excessively long or rushed timelines reduce quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOD averaged two years per MEO cost study (some up to eight years); Coast Guard reviews completed faster but unit-imposed deadlines that push reviewers to rush cause incomplete reviews. Time pressure can produce vague PWSs and poor QA plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation quality of Performance Work Statement (PWS)
rubrics_metrics.description: PWSs must be specific, complete, and include robust quality assurance plans; vague or incomplete PWSs lead to poor contracts and cost increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: early food service PWSs were vague and had poor QA resulting in poor initial contracts; MLCPAC specialists found some PWSs incomplete but usable with follow-up. Vague specs allow contractor interpretation and later add-ons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and completeness of MEO costing
rubrics_metrics.description: MEO cost determinations must be based on competent analysis and current/best available cost data, not solely standardized assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GAO found DOD used standardized assumptions rather than best cost data. Coast Guard practice omits cost of doing the study, PWS, and MEO from savings calculations, and does not routinely track contract cost increases—leading to potentially inaccurate savings figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of skilled personnel/resources to conduct studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations must provide sufficiently skilled personnel and resources to prepare management studies, PWSs, and MEOs rather than shifting the burden to inadequately trained field collateral-duty staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: G-A76 initially had staff with needed competencies but shifted reviews to field units lacking skills; reviewers often only had supplements, an example study, and a HQ contact—which is insufficient and increases time and error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordination between headquarters and contract administration
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be clear coordination and communication between headquarters study teams and local contract administrators (MLC/MLCPAC) to ensure complete, consistent reviews and solicitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distance between review staff and sites and limited coordination led to incomplete PWSs and solicitation problems; examples include limited coordination between Headquarters and MLCPAC Alameda on Pacific Area solicitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximity/engagement of study team to site
rubrics_metrics.description: Study teams should be sufficiently close or engaged with the review site to obtain needed information and produce complete PWSs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Headquarters staff had subject-matter experts available but were still distant from sites; lack of closeness contributed to incomplete PWSs. Field-conducted reviews by unskilled personnel also suffered from distance of expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: COTR qualifications, continuity, and training
rubrics_metrics.description: Contracting Officer’s Technical Representatives (COTRs) should have sufficient experience, continuity, and real-world training to perform QA and detect contractor noncompliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: COTRs often serve 2–3 years and may lack experience; short 1–5 day courses do not substitute for experience. Example: contractor giving away breakfasts should have been caught by a well-prepared COTR. Inadequate COTR attention or skill undermines contract oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality assurance (QA) enforcement and independence
rubrics_metrics.description: QA must be actively enforced by the COTR and should not rely solely on contractor assertions; COTRs must maintain appropriate professional distance from contractors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At Base Honolulu the contractor was 'running the Coast Guard' due to weak QA follow-up; some COTRs relied on contractor claims of completion. Personal closeness between COTR and contractor was identified as a problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of solicitation method appropriate to work
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose sealed bid versus RFP/negotiation based on type of work, PWS detail, and whether set-aside for small business applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most Coast Guard contracts used sealed bids when price alone determined award; RFP/negotiated processes used depending on work type and when not small-business set-aside.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and implications of small-business (8(a)) set-asides
rubrics_metrics.description: Reserving procurements under SBA 8(a) or small-business competition may simplify contracting (avoids cost comparison) and help meet small-business quotas but affects competition and award procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial Coast Guard practice reserved many contracted-out functions for 8(a) firms, making contracting-out easier and helping meet 8(a) quotas. However, set-asides change the competitive landscape and may be the only practical option in some areas (e.g., food service).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate measurement and reporting of cost savings
rubrics_metrics.description: Cost savings estimates must be based on reliable data, include all relevant costs (including study and implementation costs), and monitor actual post-implementation operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GAO found DOD’s reporting used standardized assumptions, incomplete/inaccurate databases, miscalculations, and omitted implementation costs. Coast Guard reports average annual savings but ignore contract cost increases and study costs, and do not routinely collect post-award cost data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tracking and accounting for contract cost increases
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must routinely track cost increases during contract life (e.g., wage determinations, modifications, extensions) and factor them into cost-effectiveness assessments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cost increases in case studies were primarily due to DOL wage determination adjustments and contract extensions; Coast Guard does not routinely track these increases unless performance problems arise, risking overstatement of savings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workforce impact assessment and mitigation (multi-mission impact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Management studies should include a multi-mission impact statement assessing effects on employees, morale, productivity, and mission-readiness, and plans for mitigation and placement of affected employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: COMDT now requires a multi-mission impact statement to assess employee effects. Agencies must provide 'maximum effort' reemployment assistance (priority for positions, reemployment lists, training/relocation costs, coordination with OPM/DOL, right of first refusal for contract positions). GAO found employee concern and attrition begin upon study announcement, reducing productivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring retention, reenlistment, and rating-specific impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate how contracting-out affects specific personnel specialties (e.g., Subsistence Specialist, Electronics Technician), sea/shore rotation, advancement timelines, and reenlistment/retention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: SS rating saw loss of shore billets, altered sea/shore rotation (up to 20/1), slowed advancement, and low reenlistment—measures that can indicate negative long-term retention impacts not captured by immediate cost savings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for returning functions to in-house performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish criteria for returning contracted functions to government performance, such as essential/safety-critical services, contractor default/bankruptcy, or unacceptable quality/cost performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Crash-Rescue service returned in-house after contractor bankruptcy endangered SAR operations; Petaluma food service returned due to contractor inability to match training-facility meal quality and mutual agreement not to exercise options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract specification clarity and definition of requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Specifications must be well-defined to avoid ambiguity and later add-ons that increase costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOD audits showed poorly prepared PWSs omitted tasks leading to contract add-ons and cost increases. Case studies found past specs too vague and open to interpretation—both parties cited this as a problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract administrative staffing and communication channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure contracting offices have adequate staffing and clear authorization/communication lists so COTRs and customers can place orders and get timely responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems included long distances to MLCPAC causing slow responses, unclear authorization lists, and contractors using government administrative support without compensation. Contract modifications and extensions were sometimes driven by procurement delays and limited funding availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of wage determination and funding cycles in cost estimating
rubrics_metrics.description: Cost estimates and option/extension pricing must account for Department of Labor wage determinations, potential wage increases, and government funding availability (continuing resolutions) that affect contract cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Base Honolulu contract experienced major cost increases when a DOL wage determination was incorporated during an extension, nearly doubling costs; limited government funds and continuing resolutions caused multiple contract extensions and modifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-award performance monitoring and willingness to re-evaluate
rubrics_metrics.description: After contracting-out, agencies should monitor contractor performance and be prepared to re-evaluate or return functions in-house if performance or cost-effectiveness deteriorates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coast Guard rarely returned contracted activities to in-house status (only two reported). The agency generally does not track contract cost increases unless a major performance problem arises; better post-award monitoring could identify cases warranting review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of deobligation and meal-sales-based pricing mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: For fixed-price food service contracts, pricing and deobligation mechanisms should reflect actual meal sales ranges and be monitored to manage contractor payments and obligated funds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Food service contract pricing uses meal volume ranges (higher per-meal price for lower sales); declining meals can trigger deobligation of funds. Proper invoicing and COTR confirmation of monthly sales are necessary to ensure correct obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational improvement and integration with broader quality management efforts
rubrics_metrics.description: Coordinate A-76 implementation with Total Quality Management (TQM) and in-house process reviews to seek efficiency improvements beyond contracting-out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: COMDT(G-CPP-2) tasked to review in-house operations for process improvements and coordinate with workforce planning; TQM commitment and reduced review workload can create opportunities to improve internal operations rather than defaulting to contracting-out.
